title: Understanding LLMs
description: The major model families, how to choose between them, and the limits every one of them shares.

lessons.title: The main model families
lessons.description: Who makes GPT, Gemini, Claude and Llama, and why the rest goes stale fast.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Four families of large language model come up constantly. Knowing who makes each one, and roughly what each is known for, is enough to follow any conversation about them.

A warning before the list. **Every specific claim about these models goes stale within months.** Version numbers, context sizes, prices, benchmark scores, which one is "best" -- all of it changes, often several times a year. This lesson deliberately tells you the durable things and sends you elsewhere for the rest.

### GPT, from OpenAI

The family that made this technology famous. ChatGPT, built on GPT models, is what most people mean when they say "AI" in conversation.

Broadly known for: very wide general capability, the largest ecosystem of third-party tools and integrations, and strong adoption in business.

### Gemini, from Google

Google's family, built from the start to handle more than text.

Broadly known for: multimodal work, integration with Google's own products such as Search, Docs and Gmail, and handling long inputs.

### Claude, from Anthropic

Anthropic's family. Anthropic is a company founded with an explicit focus on AI safety, and that emphasis shows in how the models behave.

Broadly known for: long-form writing and analysis, coding, and a noticeably careful tone -- more likely than some to say it is not sure, and more likely to push back on a request it thinks is a bad idea.

### Llama, from Meta

The important one in this list for a different reason: Meta publishes the weights.

That means anyone can download the model and run it on their own hardware. No API, no per-request charge, no data leaving your machine. This has made Llama the foundation of an enormous ecosystem of derived and specialised models, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

### Others worth knowing exist

**Mistral**, from a French company of the same name, with a strong open-weights line. **Qwen**, from Alibaba, also with open weights and strong multilingual results. **DeepSeek**, notable for demonstrating that strong models could be trained far more cheaply than assumed. There are many more, and the list changes.

### The honest summary

At any given moment, the leading models from the major labs are **much closer to each other than the marketing suggests**. For most everyday tasks -- writing, summarising, explaining, answering -- you would struggle to reliably tell them apart in a blind test.

Where they differ noticeably is at the edges: very long documents, difficult code, unusual languages, refusal behaviour, and tone. And which one leads at any particular edge changes with each release.

The practical conclusion: do not pick a model from a table of claims. Test the ones you can access on your own task. That is the lab at the end of this module.

## Demonstrate

Here is what a fair comparison actually looks like, and it is not a benchmark score.

Take a task you genuinely do. Say: turning a page of messy meeting notes into a structured summary with actions and owners.

Write **one prompt**. Run it, unchanged, in three tools. Put the three outputs side by side.

What you will find is not that one is right and two are wrong. You will find that one tends to over-summarise, one adds structure you did not ask for, and one hedges more. Which of those suits you is a judgement about your task and your taste, and no benchmark can make it for you.

That is the entire method, and it takes twenty minutes.

## Practice

Find, for each of the four families, one thing its maker currently claims it is good at. Use the maker's own product page.

Then, for each claim, write down how you would test it yourself in under ten minutes.

You will notice that many claims are written so that they cannot be tested -- "more capable", "industry-leading", "state of the art". Note which ones those are. That is a useful reflex to develop, and it applies well beyond AI.

## What to remember

- GPT is OpenAI, Gemini is Google, Claude is Anthropic, Llama is Meta
- Llama publishes its weights, which changes what you can do with it
- Leading models are much closer together than the marketing suggests
- Every specific claim about a model goes stale quickly, so check rather than trust a course
- Pick a model by testing it on your own task, not from a comparison table

lessons.title: Open-source and proprietary models
lessons.description: Models you use versus models you have, and the one question that decides it.
lessons.content:
## Learn

There is a real and consequential split between models you **use** and models you **have**.

### Proprietary models

You send text to a company's servers over the internet. Their model produces a response. They send it back. You pay per use, or by subscription.

GPT, Gemini and Claude are used this way.

What you get: the most capable models available, no hardware to buy, no maintenance, and improvements arriving without you doing anything.

What you give up: your text goes to someone else's computer. You cannot see how the model works. The provider can change or retire it, adjust pricing, or refuse your use case. And if their service is down, so are you.

### Open-weights models

The company publishes the trained weights. You download them and run the model on hardware you control.

Llama, Mistral and Qwen have lines like this.

What you get: your data never leaves your machine, which settles a great many privacy and compliance conversations immediately. No per-request cost. No dependency on anyone else's uptime or pricing. You can modify the model. And a version you have downloaded cannot be taken away from you.

What you give up: you need the hardware, and capable models need serious hardware. You do the maintenance. And the very best models at any moment are usually proprietary, though the gap has narrowed considerably.

### The name is a bit of a lie

These are usually called "open source" models. Mostly they are not.

Open source, properly, means you can see and modify the source -- which for a model would mean the training data and the training code. Almost nobody publishes those. What is published is the **weights**: the finished numbers.

The honest term is **open weights**. You get the result of the training, not the means to reproduce it. Several also come with licence conditions restricting commercial use, which is another thing open source would not do.

This matters when someone tells you a model is "open source" as though that settles a question about transparency. It usually does not.

### How to actually decide

One question does most of the work: **can this data leave your building?**

If it cannot -- patient records, unreleased financials, legally privileged material, personal data under a strict regime -- then a local open-weights model is not a preference, it is the only option, and the capability gap is a cost you accept.

If it can, use the proprietary models. They are more capable, they need no infrastructure, and you have better things to do than maintain a server.

Cost only becomes the deciding factor at high volume, and it is a real crossover: at enough requests, running your own becomes cheaper. Most people never reach that point.

## Demonstrate

Three organisations, three correct and different answers.

**A hospital** wants to summarise clinical notes. The data cannot leave their systems. They run an open-weights model on their own hardware, accept that it is somewhat less capable, and put a clinician in the loop. Correct decision.

**A four-person startup** wants AI features in their product. No unusual data sensitivity, no hardware, no spare engineer. They call a proprietary API and ship in a week. Correct decision.

**A large retailer** classifies millions of product descriptions a month. The data is not sensitive; the volume is enormous. At their scale, per-request pricing costs more than running their own. They fine-tune an open-weights model and run it themselves. Correct decision.

Notice that none of these decisions was about which model was better.

## Practice

Take an organisation you know -- your employer, your college department, a society, a family business.

Write down three tasks AI could help with. For each one, answer these in order:

1. What data goes into the model?
2. Can that data leave the building? Say why, referring to an actual rule or risk rather than a feeling.
3. Roughly how many requests a month?
4. Open weights or proprietary, and why?

Most people find that questions 1 and 2 decide almost everything, and question 3 rarely matters. If your answers all come out the same way, that is a normal and correct result.

## What to remember

- Proprietary means using someone else's model over the internet; open weights means running your own
- "Open source" is usually the wrong term -- weights are published, training data and code are not
- The deciding question is almost always whether the data can leave your building
- Cost only decides at high volume, and most people never get there
- Some open-weights licences restrict commercial use, so read them

lessons.title: Choosing a model for a job
lessons.description: Five factors, and the one step everybody skips.
lessons.content:
## Learn

"Which model is best?" is the wrong question, because it has no answer. "Which model is right for this job?" has one, and it is usually easy to reach.

Five things decide it.

### 1. Can the data leave your building?

Covered in the last lesson, and it comes first because it can end the conversation. If the answer is no, you are choosing among models you can run yourself, and nothing else on this list overrides that.

### 2. How hard is the task?

This matters more than people expect, and in the opposite direction to their instinct.

Most real tasks are not hard. Classifying a message, extracting a date, rewriting a sentence, answering a question from a supplied document -- a small, cheap, fast model does these as well as an expensive one.

The expensive models earn their cost on genuinely difficult work: multi-step reasoning, subtle code, long documents where a detail on page forty matters on page two.

Using the most capable model for everything is the most common and most expensive mistake in this area. Start small, and move up only when you can point at something the small model actually got wrong.

### 3. How much text is involved?

If you are feeding in long documents, the amount the model can consider at once becomes the binding constraint, and some families handle long inputs better than others.

For short exchanges this does not matter at all.

### 4. How fast does it need to be?

A person waiting for a chat response tolerates a few seconds. A model in the middle of a checkout flow does not have a few seconds. Smaller models are faster, and for interactive uses that often matters more than the last few points of quality.

### 5. What does it cost at your volume?

Ten requests a day: cost is irrelevant, use whatever is best. Ten million a month: cost may be the whole decision.

Work out which of those you are before spending any time on it. People agonise over pricing for workloads that will cost a few pounds a month.

### The method that actually works

1. Write down the task, precisely
2. Build a small set of **real** examples with the answers you want -- ten to twenty is enough
3. Run them through two or three candidate models with the same prompt
4. Compare against your answers
5. Pick the cheapest one that is good enough

Step 2 is the one people skip, and it is the one that makes the whole thing work. Without it you are comparing vibes.

And note "good enough", not "best". If the cheap model gets nineteen of twenty right and the expensive one gets twenty, whether that last one is worth five times the cost depends entirely on what happens when it is wrong.

## Demonstrate

A support team wants to route incoming emails into five categories.

**The wrong approach.** Read comparison articles. Pick the model with the best benchmark scores. Build on it. Discover months later that it costs far more than needed and that nobody ever checked its accuracy on the actual emails.

**The right approach.** Take fifty real emails and label them by hand -- an hour's work. Write one prompt. Run all fifty through a small model and a large one. Compare against the labels.

A very common result: the small model gets forty-six right, the large model gets forty-eight, and the large model costs several times more. Now the decision is concrete. Two extra errors in fifty, against the cost difference at your volume, with a known consequence for a misrouted email. That is a decision a person can actually make.

The hour spent labelling is what turned an unanswerable question into an easy one.

## Practice

Pick a task you would genuinely use a model for.

Build the evaluation set. Ten examples is enough to start. For each, write the input and the output you would consider correct. Do this **before** you look at any model, so you are not marking to what you were given.

Then run all ten through two different tools with the same prompt, and score them against your answers.

Write down: how many each got right, which was faster, and which you would choose. Keep this -- it is the core of the assignment at the end of this module, and it is a genuinely useful professional habit.

## What to remember

- "Which is best" has no answer; "which is right for this job" usually does
- Data sensitivity comes first and can end the decision on its own
- Most tasks are easy, and using the most capable model for everything is an expensive habit
- Build a small set of real examples with known answers, then compare
- Choose the cheapest model that is good enough, not the best one available

lessons.title: Multimodal AI
lessons.description: Excellent at meaning, unreliable at precision.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A multimodal model handles more than one kind of input or output. In practice this usually means it accepts images as well as text, and often audio, documents or video too.

The change is bigger than it sounds. Before, if you wanted to ask a question about a photograph, you needed one model to describe the photograph and another to answer the question, with all the loss that passing through a description involves. Now one model looks at the image and answers.

### What you can actually do with it

**Ask questions about an image.** What is in this photo, what does this diagram show, what is wrong with this chart.

**Read text from an image.** Handwriting, a photographed receipt, a screenshot, a whiteboard. This is optical character recognition with comprehension attached: it does not just transcribe, it understands what it transcribed.

**Understand documents visually.** Hand it a PDF with tables and charts and it reads the layout, not just the words. This matters enormously for anything with structure.

**Work from a screenshot.** Show it an error message, a spreadsheet, a user interface, a design, and ask what to do about it.

**Audio in.** Transcribe, summarise a recording, answer questions about what was said.

### The one to build a habit around

**Photograph it rather than describe it.** People type long descriptions of things they could simply show. A photograph of an error message is faster to produce and far more informative than a paragraph of "it says something about a module not being found".

Once this becomes a reflex, it changes how you use these tools day to day more than any other single habit in this course.

### Where it falls down

**Small text and fine detail.** Numbers in a dense table, a small footnote, a low-resolution screenshot. It may read them wrong, and it will not tell you it is unsure.

**Precise spatial reasoning.** Exact positions, precise counting of many similar objects, careful measurement. Counting is a particular weak spot.

**Reading charts precisely.** It will describe a trend well and misread a specific value confidently. Never take a number off a chart without checking it against the underlying data.

**Anything where being slightly wrong matters.** The failure mode is the same as everywhere in this course: a confident, plausible, wrong answer, with nothing marking it as different from a right one.

## Demonstrate

Try all four of these. They take a couple of minutes each and between them they map the capability well.

1. **Photograph a handwritten page** -- your own notes, a shopping list -- and ask the model to type it up. Check it against the original word by word.
2. **Screenshot a chart** from a news article and ask what it shows. Then ask for three specific values, and check them.
3. **Photograph a real object** -- the contents of a fridge, a bookshelf -- and ask a question that needs actual attention, such as what you could cook, or how many books are on the second shelf.
4. **Screenshot an error message** from any piece of software and ask what it means.

You will very likely find 1 and 4 excellent, 2 good on the trend and unreliable on the numbers, and 3 good on the qualitative question and poor on the count.

That pattern -- excellent at meaning, unreliable at precision -- is the thing to carry with you.

## Practice

Find a real task in your own life or work where photographing something would be faster than describing it.

Do it. Record what you asked, what you got, and whether it was right.

Then deliberately find the limit: give it something with small text, or a lot to count, or a precise number to read, and see where it breaks.

Write two sentences on which kinds of visual questions you would trust and which you would always check.

## What to remember

- Multimodal means more than one kind of input or output, usually images alongside text
- Photographing something is often faster and better than describing it
- Excellent at meaning, unreliable at precision
- Counting and reading exact values off charts are known weak spots
- Wrong answers look exactly like right ones, as always

lessons.title: Hallucinations, in depth
lessons.description: Where it clusters, five defences that work and one that does not.
lessons.content:
## Learn

You met hallucination in module 1 and learned in module 2 where it comes from. This lesson is about what to actually do.

### The one-line explanation

A model produces likely continuations. It has no mechanism for checking truth. When the likely continuation is false, you get a false statement, delivered exactly like a true one.

That is it. There is nothing else going on. Which means hallucination is not a bug to be fixed in some future version -- it is the normal operation of the system producing an output you did not want.

### Where it happens most

Hallucination is not evenly spread. It clusters in predictable places, and knowing them is most of the defence.

**Citations and references.** Papers, books, legal cases, standards, page numbers. The format of a citation is extremely predictable, which makes fabricating one easy and convincing. Treat every single citation as unverified until you have found it.

**Specific numbers.** Statistics, dates, prices, measurements, version numbers. A plausible number is easy to produce and hard to spot.

**Details about real people.** Job titles, affiliations, what someone said, career history. Also the area where being wrong does the most harm.

**Niche technical detail.** Functions that do not exist in a library, options a tool does not have, configuration that looks right and is not. Common in coding, and usually caught quickly because the code fails -- which makes it one of the safer places for it to happen.

**Anything after the knowledge cutoff.** The next lesson.

**Anything that does not exist.** Ask about a non-existent book, law or product and you will often get a detailed description rather than "that does not exist". The model has no way to distinguish "I have not seen this" from "this is not a thing".

### Where it happens least

**Transformation of text you supplied.** Summarising, rewriting, translating, reformatting, extracting from a document in front of it. The material is right there, so there is much less room to invent. Not zero -- a summary can still assert something the document did not say -- but far less.

This is the single most useful practical distinction in the whole course. **Asking a model to recall is risky. Asking it to transform is much safer.** Structure your work around that and most of the problem goes away.

### Five defences that work

**1. Supply the source.** Paste the document and ask questions about it, rather than asking from memory. This converts recall into transformation.

**2. Give it permission to not know.** Add: *"If you are not certain, say so. Do not guess."* This genuinely reduces confident invention. It does not eliminate it.

**3. Verify every citation, number and name.** Not a sample. Every one. This is tedious and it is the job.

**4. Ask the same thing in a fresh conversation.** Invented details vary between runs; real ones tend not to. Different answers are a strong signal something is fabricated. Identical answers are weaker evidence than you would like, but the test is cheap.

**5. Notice unusual specificity.** A model that produces a precise figure, a page number and an exact date for something obscure is more likely inventing than remembering. Real recall on obscure material is usually vaguer.

### One defence that does not work

**Asking the model whether it is sure.** This produces more plausible text about certainty. There is no confidence signal inside the system for it to report. A model will confidently affirm a fabrication, and it will sometimes retract something true because you sounded doubtful.

## Demonstrate

A three-part test that takes five minutes and teaches the whole lesson.

**Part one.** Ask any tool: *"Tell me about the 2019 Dhanraj Committee report on urban transport."* There is no such report. Note whether it says so, or produces a summary.

**Part two.** Ask the same question again with: *"If this does not exist or you are not certain, say so."* Compare. You will usually get a better answer, and this is the cheapest single improvement available to you.

**Part three.** Now take something real -- a document you have -- and paste it in, asking a question about its contents. Notice how much more reliable it is.

Those three runs are recall, guarded recall, and transformation. The difference between them is most of what you need to know.

## Practice

Take a piece of work you would genuinely ask an AI to help with. Write the prompt you would naturally have written.

Now rewrite it twice:

1. A version that **supplies the source material** instead of relying on recall
2. A version that **explicitly permits uncertainty**

Run all three. Record the differences.

Then take the best output and mark every factual claim in it with a highlighter. Verify each one. Count how many you could confirm, how many you could not, and how long it took.

That count is the real cost of using these tools on factual work, and most people have never measured it.

## What to remember

- Hallucination is the normal mechanism producing an unwanted output, not a fixable bug
- It clusters in citations, numbers, details about people, and anything that does not exist
- Asking a model to transform supplied text is far safer than asking it to recall
- Supplying the source and permitting uncertainty are the two cheapest big wins
- Asking the model whether it is sure does not work and never will

lessons.title: Knowledge cutoff and other limits
lessons.description: The hard edge of training data, and what search does and does not fix.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Every model was trained on material gathered up to a point in time. That point is the **knowledge cutoff**, and it is a hard edge.

Before it, the model has seen a great deal. After it, nothing.

### The part that causes trouble

A model does not reliably know where its own edge is.

Ask about something from after the cutoff and you might get "I do not have information about that". You might equally get a confident, detailed, entirely invented answer -- because a plausible continuation exists whether or not the model saw the facts.

So the cutoff is not a wall the model stops at. It is a line past which its output stops being connected to anything.

### Search changes this, and introduces its own problem

Many tools now search the web and feed results to the model. This genuinely helps: the model can work with current material.

But it moves the problem rather than removing it. Now the answer is only as good as what the search returned. If the search finds a bad source, an outdated page or a piece of marketing, the model will summarise it fluently and you will get a confident answer built on a poor foundation.

So with search, ask a different question: not "does it know this" but **"where did this come from"**. If the tool shows sources, look at them. A fluent answer over three weak sources is worse than no answer, because it is convincing.

### Other limits worth knowing

**It does not know what it does not know.** There is no internal sense of "I have not seen much about this". Sparse knowledge and rich knowledge produce equally confident output.

**It does not know today's date** unless told. Ask it to calculate an age or a deadline and it may use a date from its training.

**It cannot do anything outside the conversation** unless given tools. It cannot check your calendar, read your files or send an email unless a tool has been connected, which is module 11.

**It is not reliably consistent.** Ask the same question twice, get two answers. For creative work this is fine. For anything that needs to be repeatable it is a real problem.

**It cannot reliably count or do careful arithmetic.** It produces likely-looking numbers. For anything that matters, use a calculator, or a tool that runs actual code.

**It cannot tell you why it said something.** Ask for its reasoning and you get a plausible explanation generated after the fact, not an account of what happened inside. This is worth knowing before you rely on a model to justify a decision.

## Demonstrate

Four quick probes. Run them on any tool and note which limit each one exposes.

1. *"What is today's date?"* -- does it know, or guess?
2. *"What significant events happened in the last two weeks?"* -- does it decline, search, or invent?
3. *"Multiply 8,472 by 391."* -- check it on a calculator.
4. Ask a question, then in a **new** conversation ask the identical question. Compare.

Then, if your tool supports search, ask something current and look at the sources. Click at least one. Judge whether you would have cited it yourself.

That last step is the one almost nobody does, and it is where the value is.

## Practice

Write down five questions you would want to ask an AI tool in your own study or work.

For each, mark which of these applies:

- **Safe**: the answer does not depend on recent events, exact numbers, or specific sources
- **Needs search**: the answer depends on current information
- **Needs verification**: the answer involves citations, statistics, or details about real people
- **Should not use AI**: the cost of a confident wrong answer is too high

Be honest about the fourth category. Most people have at least one, and finding it is the point of the exercise.

## What to remember

- Every model has a knowledge cutoff and does not reliably know where it is
- Search helps, but moves the problem to the quality of what was found
- The model does not know today's date, cannot count reliably, and cannot explain its own reasoning
- Ask the same question twice to check consistency; it is cheap and revealing
- Sort your questions by which limit they run into before you ask them

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
These cover the whole of module 3. Answer first, then check, and read every explanation.

:::quiz
Q. Which company makes Claude?
- Google
- OpenAI
+ Anthropic
- Meta
= GPT is OpenAI, Gemini is Google, Claude is Anthropic, Llama is Meta. Knowing who makes what is durable; almost every other specific claim about these models goes stale within months.

Q. What does it actually mean when a model is described as "open source"?
- The training data and training code are published
+ Usually only the trained weights are published, which is better called open weights
- Anyone can use it commercially without restriction
- It is free to run
= Open source properly means the source is available, which for a model would be the training data and code. Almost nobody publishes those. What is published is the finished numbers. Several such models also carry licences restricting commercial use.

Q. Which question should come first when choosing a model?
- Which model scores highest on benchmarks
- Which model is cheapest per request
+ Whether the data is allowed to leave your building
- Which model has the largest context window
= Data sensitivity can end the decision on its own. If the data cannot leave, you are choosing among models you can run yourself, and no capability or cost argument overrides that.

Q. What is the most common and most expensive mistake in model selection?
- Choosing an open-weights model when a proprietary one would do
+ Using the most capable model for tasks that a small one handles just as well
- Testing on too few examples
- Ignoring the context window
= Most real tasks are easy. Classifying, extracting, rewriting and answering from a supplied document are done as well by small, fast, cheap models. The capable models earn their cost on genuinely hard work, and defaulting to them for everything is expensive.

Q. What is the step people skip when comparing models, and why does it matter?
- Reading the provider's documentation
+ Building a small set of real examples with known correct answers
- Measuring response latency
- Checking the licence
= Without labelled examples you are comparing impressions. Ten to twenty real examples with the answers you want turns an unanswerable question into an easy one, and it usually takes about an hour.

Q. For which kind of task is a multimodal model least reliable?
- Explaining what a diagram shows
- Transcribing handwriting
+ Reading an exact value off a chart
- Interpreting an error message in a screenshot
= The pattern is excellent at meaning, unreliable at precision. It will describe a trend well and misread a specific number confidently. Counting many similar objects is the other classic weak spot.

Q. Which of these substantially reduces hallucination?
- Asking the model whether it is certain
+ Pasting the source document and asking questions about it
- Using a model with more parameters
- Asking the question more politely
= Supplying the source converts recall into transformation, and transformation is far safer because the material is right there. Asking about certainty just produces more plausible text; there is no confidence signal inside the system to report.

Q. Where does hallucination cluster most?
- Summarising a document you supplied
- Rewriting a paragraph in a different tone
+ Citations, specific numbers, and details about real people
- Translating between languages
= These have highly predictable formats, which makes convincing fabrication easy. Transformation of supplied text is the much safer category. Details about real people are also where being wrong does the most harm.

Q. A tool with web search gives you a confident, fluent answer about a current event. What should you check?
- Whether the model has a recent knowledge cutoff
+ What sources the search actually returned, and whether they are any good
- Whether the model is multimodal
- How many parameters the model has
= Search moves the problem rather than removing it. The answer is only as good as what was found. A fluent summary of three weak sources is worse than no answer, because it is convincing. Click at least one source.

Q. You ask a model to explain why it gave a particular answer. What are you getting?
- A record of the computation it performed
- The relevant part of its training data
+ A plausible explanation generated after the fact
- Its confidence scores in readable form
= The model has no access to an account of its own processing. It produces text that plausibly explains the answer, which is a different thing and may not correspond to anything that happened. Worth knowing before relying on a model to justify a decision.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for module 4. Fewer than seven, revisit the lesson covering what you missed. Module 4 assumes you are comfortable with hallucination and with the recall-versus-transformation distinction in particular.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: one prompt, four models
lessons.description: Compare three tools on a task you actually do, with a real evaluation set.
lessons.content:
This lab takes about thirty-five minutes and produces something genuinely useful: a comparison of the models you can actually access, on a task you actually do.

## Before you start

Pick **three** tools you can access. Any three of ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude and Perplexity work. Each has offered a free tier; check what each currently offers before you start.

Open all three in separate tabs. Have a document open for recording.

## Step 1: Choose a real task

Not a puzzle, not a trick question. Something you genuinely do.

Good choices: turn messy notes into a structured summary; rewrite a paragraph for a specific audience; extract structured fields from a block of text; explain a concept from your field to a beginner; draft a reply to an awkward email.

Write the task down in one sentence before continuing.

## Step 2: Build a small evaluation set

This is the step that makes the lab worth doing.

Create **five** real inputs for your task. Real ones -- actual notes, actual paragraphs, actual emails, anonymised if needed.

For each, write down what a good output looks like. Not the exact words; the things that must be true. For a meeting summary that might be: every action item captured, each with an owner, under 150 words, no invented commitments.

Do this **before** you run anything, so you are not marking to what you happen to be given.

## Step 3: Write one prompt

One prompt, used unchanged in all three tools. If you tune the prompt per tool you are comparing prompts, not models.

Include the task, any constraints, and the output format you want.

## Step 4: Run it

Five inputs, three tools, fifteen runs. Use a fresh conversation for each run so nothing carries over.

Record, for each run: the output, roughly how long it took, and whether it met each of the criteria you wrote in step 2.

## Step 5: Score it

Build a simple tally. For each tool: how many of the five met all your criteria, how many partly, how many failed.

Then note the qualitative differences, which are usually more interesting than the score:

- Which was most verbose? Which most concise?
- Which added structure you did not ask for?
- Which followed your format instruction most exactly?
- Which hedged most? Which was most confident?
- Did any invent anything? Check carefully.

:::hint All three did fine and I cannot tell them apart
That is a real and common result, and it is worth knowing -- it means for this task, pick on price, speed or convenience. If you want to find a difference, make the task harder: a longer input, a stricter format, a subtler constraint, or something that needs a detail from the start of a long document. Differences show up at the edges, not in the middle.
:::

## Step 6: Probe one limit

Pick one and run it across all three:

- Ask for three sources on a topic in your field, then verify every one
- Ask about something from the last two weeks and see which searches, declines or invents
- Give all three the same arithmetic problem and check on a calculator
- Ask one question, then ask it again in a fresh conversation, and compare

Record which tools handled it well.

## Step 7: Write it up

Six short paragraphs:

1. Your task and your five criteria
2. The scores, as actual numbers
3. The qualitative differences you noticed
4. The limit you probed, and which tools handled it
5. Which tool you would use for this task, and why
6. What would change your mind

The sixth is the most important and the one people leave out. If you cannot say what evidence would change your answer, you have not made a decision, you have picked a favourite.

## What good looks like

Strong write-ups have **numbers and quotations**. "Tool B was better" is weak. "Tool B met all five criteria, Tool A met three -- both times it missed, it dropped the owner from an action item, for example turning 'Priya to send the draft' into 'the draft will be sent'" is strong.

Strong write-ups also report when nothing separated the tools. That is a finding, not a failed lab.

lessons.title: Assignment: a model selection brief
lessons.description: A recommendation a manager could act on, marked against a published rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Write a **model selection brief**: a short document recommending which model a real organisation should use for a real task, with the evidence behind it.

This is a document a manager could act on. Write it that way.

## Choose a real situation

Name an actual organisation and an actual task. Your employer, your college department, a society, a small business, a family business.

If you genuinely cannot use a real one, invent one -- but give it specific constraints: a size, a sector, a data policy, a budget, a volume. A vague organisation produces a vague brief and loses marks throughout.

## What to submit

One document, **nine hundred to thirteen hundred words**, in these six sections.

### 1. The task

What exactly is the model being asked to do? One paragraph, specific enough that someone could build it. "Help with customer service" is not a task. "Classify incoming support emails into five named categories and draft a first-response for the three most common" is.

### 2. The constraints

Four, at minimum, each with a reason:

- **Data sensitivity.** What goes in, and can it leave the building? Cite an actual policy, regulation or risk, not a feeling.
- **Volume.** Roughly how many requests, and over what period. An estimate with a stated basis.
- **Latency.** Is anyone waiting? How long is acceptable?
- **Cost of error.** What happens when it is wrong, who notices, and how quickly?

### 3. The candidates

Two or three specific options, described at family level. Say why each is a plausible candidate for **these** constraints. Do not list every model that exists.

Avoid quoting prices, context sizes or version numbers as facts. They change. Say what you would check and where.

### 4. The evidence

The section that separates a brief from an opinion.

Describe your evaluation set: how many examples, where they came from, what a correct answer looked like. Then report what happened, with numbers.

Minimum: **ten examples across two models**. You can reuse and extend the lab.

Include at least one example in full -- the input, each model's output, and your judgement -- so a reader can check your marking.

### 5. The recommendation

One model, stated plainly, with the reasoning tied to the constraints in section 2 and the evidence in section 4.

Include what you are **giving up** by choosing it. Every real choice has a cost; a recommendation that claims none has not been thought through.

### 6. What would change this

Two or three specific things that would make you revisit: a volume threshold, a change in data policy, a failure rate you would not tolerate, a capability the task might grow to need.

Give numbers where you can. "If volume passed about fifty thousand a month" is useful. "If things changed" is not.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**Task definition, 10 marks.** Full marks for a task specific enough to build from. Few marks for a description that could mean several different systems.

**Constraints, 20 marks.** Full marks where all four are present, each with a reason grounded in something real. Marks are lost for constraints asserted without basis, and especially for a data-sensitivity claim with no policy or risk behind it.

**Candidates, 10 marks.** Full marks for two or three options genuinely suited to these constraints, with no stale specifics stated as fact. Marks are lost for listing models without connecting them to the constraints.

**Evidence, 30 marks.** Full marks for at least ten real examples across two models, with a stated marking scheme, results as numbers, and one worked example shown in full. This section carries the most weight because it is the whole point. A brief with no evidence cannot score above half overall, however well written.

**Recommendation, 20 marks.** Full marks where the choice follows visibly from sections 2 and 4 and the tradeoff is stated honestly. Marks are lost where the recommendation does not follow from the evidence presented, and where no cost is acknowledged.

**What would change it, 10 marks.** Full marks for two or three specific, numbered triggers. Few marks for vague conditions.

## What will cost you marks

**Recommending the most capable model without evidence that the task needs it.** This is the most common failure, and module 3 exists largely to prevent it. If your evidence shows a smaller model is good enough, recommend it.

**Quoting figures that will be wrong next quarter.** Prices, context sizes, benchmark scores, version numbers. Say what you would check and where, not what it costs today.

**An evidence section that is really an opinion section.** "I tried both and preferred X" is not evidence. Numbers against known answers are.

**A recommendation with no stated downside.** There is always one. Naming it is what makes the brief trustworthy.

:::hint I cannot get access to two different models
Most general-purpose assistants have offered a free tier, so two is usually achievable. If you genuinely have access to only one, compare that model against itself at two different levels of prompting -- a bare instruction versus a carefully constructed one with examples and constraints. The comparison method is identical, the evidence is just as real, and you will often find the prompt matters more than the model. Say in the brief that this is what you did and why.
:::
